To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
local nonfamily social organization and the size of the community are important predictors of the consumption of environmental goods and services.

1) the size of local nonfamily organizations, such as clubs and associations, is positively related to the amount of indirect consumption, 2) this relationship holds after controlling for the effects of household size and affluence on indirect consumption, 3) this relationship is not due to the effects of household affluence or household size on the size of nonfamily organizations, and 4) this relationship is stronger for indirect consumption of natural resources (e.g., electricity, fuelwood,

(1) the size of local nonfamily organizations is a significant determinant of household size and consumption of environmental resources; (2) the size of the local nonfamily organization is a significant determinant, through household size and consumption, of the level of environmental degradation in the local community; (3) the effect of the size of local organizations on environmental degradation is mediated through household consumption and household size; (4) the effects of local organizations on household consumption and household composition are stronger in more affluent communities
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how and why the transition to more indirect consumption takes place.
the question of how the social organization of communities influences individual consumption behavior.
how social organization influences the way in which people interact with their natural environment.

social organization is an important determinant of the transition from direct, subsistence-level consumption to indirect, market-level consumption.
the results of this study suggest that the social organization of the local community is an important determinant of the environmental impact of household consumption.
social organization is important in determining environmental quality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are developing a theory of environmental quality that is rooted in the local community and its organization.
we find that the social context of consumption is an important determinant of the environmental impacts of consumption.
we find that the community context of consumption matters, but the specific mechanisms are not yet fully understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the community context of households is an important determinant of the environmental impacts of consumption.
the social organization of the community in which one lives can be a significant predictor of the environmental impacts of one’s household.
the social context in which consumption occurs can be a key determinant of environmental consumption, even when the social context does not directly affect individual incomes or wealth.
